frameworks.name: Level Up Before Plateau
frameworks.definition: Identify when you have maxed out a market or venture, then transition 95% of focus to the next larger challenge while keeping the prior on autopilot at 5% effort.

frameworks.name: Stay Ready So You Don't Need to Get Ready
frameworks.definition: Maintain daily cognitive, physical, emotional, and social readiness so you can capitalize on unplannable opportunities (regulatory shifts, new platforms, cultural movements) the moment they appear.

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (co-founder/CEO of Bloom Nutrition, 2016-2026) observed that every phase of exceptional performance in his career corresponded to periods of 100% focused attention on a single venture; diversified attention was consistently associated with slower growth and weaker execution.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: founder-led consumer brand
high-growth phase
claims.mechanism: When attention is not divided, decisions sharpen and execution accelerates; partners (retail buyers, distributors, co-founders) can detect commitment level and preferentially partner with fully committed operators.
bounded_by: May not apply once a business is fully systematized and can run without founder attention

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia asserts that ultra-high-net-worth individuals in their 30s and 40s universally hold concentrated single-bet portfolios rather than diversified ones; his friend Leo, then a Wall Street biotech deal salesperson calling thousands of high-net-worth individuals daily, reported that they do extensive diligence on one deal and bet the house, in contrast to the diversified portfolio advice commonly taught.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: early-stage founder with recovery runway (under 40)
high-conviction opportunity identified
claims.mechanism: Concentrated bets generate outsized returns because all resources and attention compound on a single compounding lever; diversification reduces peak upside in exchange for downside protection that young founders do not yet need.
bounded_by: Speaker acknowledges this may not apply after age 50 when recovery from zero is harder

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia argues that a small venture (e.g., $100k/year) and a large venture (e.g., $100M+/year) consume roughly equal amounts of stress, sleepless nights, and founder effort; therefore the expected-value calculation strongly favors going after the larger opportunity.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: founder choosing between opportunity sizes at the beginning of a venture
claims.mechanism: Operational complexity, team management, sales cycles, and psychological toll are largely independent of total addressable market size; the ceiling of reward scales without a matching increase in cost.
bounded_by: LaVecchia notes this is his personal observation across people he knows; not drawn from a controlled study

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition, 2019-2024) found that building in public by sharing business milestones on social media consistently attracted talent, strategic partners, retail buyers, and investors who were looking for the next big thing; he observed almost no downside to this practice.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: consumer brand founder
genuine business milestones to share (Amazon rankings, retailer placement, unit sales)
claims.mechanism: Public documentation of progress functions as a low-cost broadcast signal that filters for aligned partners and talent; people who want to join or partner with a rising brand self-select in when they can observe momentum.
bounded_by: LaVecchia distinguishes personal/sacred matters (kept private) from business achievements (shared publicly)

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia argues that entering an existing product category rather than creating a new one is more capital-efficient because marketing spend does not need to fund consumer education about what the product is; Bloom never created a new category and has been profitable every day for 10 years.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: consumer packaged goods brand
existing category with demonstrated demand
claims.mechanism: When consumers already understand a product type (greens powder, energy drink, protein), marketing budget converts directly to differentiation and trial rather than being split between category education and brand education; this reduces CAC and accelerates profitability.
bounded_by: Speaker acknowledges some timing risk: entering too late means competing against entrenched leaders with large marketing budgets

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia describes a two-phase leveling-up transition strategy: at peak performance in the current venture, allocate 95% of effort to the new larger challenge while keeping the prior venture on autopilot at 5% effort; once traction develops in the new venture, shift to 100% focus there and let the prior decline.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: current venture approaching or at market ceiling
founder has identified a larger adjacent challenge
claims.mechanism: Timing the transition at the top of the growth curve (rather than the decline) means the prior business retains enough momentum to sustain itself at reduced attention while the new venture gains initial traction.
bounded_by: Assumes the founder can identify peak before decline; missing the peak risks transitioning into a collapsing prior business that demands more than 5% attention

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (Bloom Nutrition, 2020-2024) argues that physical, cognitive, and social readiness maintained as a daily discipline creates the conditions for capitalizing on unplannable macro opportunities; Bloom exploited COVID-19 consumer behavior shifts, early TikTok adoption, GLP-1 dietary changes, and TikTok Shop launch because Bloom was already prepared to move, while larger competitors were still reacting.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
claims.speaker_term: stay ready so you don't need to get ready
conditions: consumer brand in a fast-moving cultural category
founder operating at high daily readiness
claims.mechanism: Macro opportunities (platform launches, regulatory shifts, cultural trends) occur unpredictably and close fast; organizations whose daily operational readiness is high can respond in days while bureaucratic competitors respond in months, capturing disproportionate first-mover share.

numbers.axis: unplannable opportunities capitalized on by Bloom (2019-2024)

anchors.value: doubled down on protein and greens via e-commerce while brick-and-mortar competitors were shut down
built largest in-house influencer program inside a consumer brand; 12 billion+ views
launched clear protein and low-calorie energy drinks matching GLP-1 user dietary needs
14,000+ cases of Shirley Temple energy drink sold before retail launch; major competitors not yet present

bounded_by: Does not apply to businesses in slow-moving regulated industries where speed is less determinative

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia argues that physical relocation to cities aligned with your business category directly increases the probability of high-value opportunity encounters; Bloom moved five times in five years (Philadelphia to New York to LA to Boulder to Austin) specifically tracking where the highest-leverage relationships for each business phase were concentrated.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: early-stage founder under 35 with geographic flexibility
business stage where relationship quality is a binding constraint
claims.mechanism: Physical presence in cities where the highest-density network of relevant operators, buyers, and partners concentrate increases the rate of serendipitous high-value encounters; this compounds over time as each encounter seeds the next.

numbers.axis: relocations by Bloom founders relative to business phase

anchors.value: moved to LA where influencer density was highest

anchors.region: beverage launch with Dr. Pepper and Nutribolt partnership
anchors.value: moved to Austin, Texas where Dr. Pepper and Nutribolt are headquartered

bounded_by: LaVecchia acknowledges not everyone can relocate; however frames it as the easiest controllable luck variable for those who can

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia asserts that skills, relationships, and negotiation experience from small ventures directly transfer to large ventures; learnings compound rather than reset at each scale transition.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: sequential venture builder who stays within adjacent categories
claims.mechanism: The same cognitive and interpersonal skills used in early small-scale negotiations (supplier terms, retailer placements, partnership structures) are the same muscles exercised in large-scale negotiations; early low-stakes repetitions build pattern recognition that transfers to high-stakes applications.
bounded_by: Transfer is strongest when ventures are in adjacent categories; radical industry pivots may require rebuilding domain-specific knowledge from scratch

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia claims that being in environments where you are the least capable person (not the shark in the pond) in your peer group, city, and media consumption accelerates growth; being the top performer in a low-caliber environment decreases your growth rate and luck.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: early-career founder seeking maximum growth rate
claims.mechanism: Peer group and environment establish your reference frame for what is possible and normal; a low-caliber reference frame suppresses ambition and reduces the density of high-value opportunities through which you can encounter mentors and partners.

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia argues that worrying about competitors stealing your ideas is unjustified because execution quality, not idea novelty, determines success; anyone who copies an idea will not execute it as well as the originator, who has already implemented it.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
claims.speaker_term: no one will steal your ideas
conditions: consumer brand sharing operational and strategic milestones publicly
claims.mechanism: Execution involves accumulated domain knowledge, relationships, brand trust, and operational systems that cannot be transferred via idea alone; the idea itself is a small fraction of what produces results.
bounded_by: May not apply to highly replicable digital products or proprietary formulations where IP protection is the primary moat

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia observes that Bloom's top-selling pre-workout flavors (Crisp Apple and Glacier Crush) from six to seven years ago became the number-one selling flavors in Bloom's energy drink line, illustrating that consumer preference data and brand equity accumulated in earlier products carries forward into successor product lines.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: same brand expanding across adjacent product categories
same core consumer base retained across transitions
claims.mechanism: Consumer palate preferences and brand associations built in earlier products inform product-market fit predictions for successor products; the brand equity accumulated with early adopters lowers the marketing cost of launching adjacent products to the same audience.
bounded_by: Requires brand continuity and audience retention across product transitions; does not apply if brand is rebuilt from scratch for each new category

examples.text: Greg LaVecchia and his wife Mari started by selling instant-download PDFs as a fitness business from their college dorm room with no capital. They scaled it to a couple million dollars annually, then used those learnings to launch physical products starting with booty bands, selling roughly a million units at ~$20 each. With consumer demand and trust established, they launched Bloom starting with a female pre-workout in 2019, expanded into recovery powders and greens powder (bootstrapping the greens business to $180M), then made the counterintuitive move of launching an energy drink to compete with Monster, Red Bull, and Celsius. By 2026, Bloom's energy drink was available in 70,000 doors via Dr. Pepper distribution and the Shirley Temple soda was in ~40,000 doors. LaVecchia frames each transition as deliberately leaving behind a good business to pursue a great one, with the energy drink business doing more in a single day than the booty band business did in an entire week.

When COVID-19 hit in 2020, Bloom was in Brooklyn with e-commerce channels already established via Shopify and Amazon. While competitors with large corporate offices were shut down and scrambling to set up remote work via Zoom, Bloom immediately doubled down on protein (for at-home baking) and greens powder (for at-home wellness), riding both to strong sales before any competitor could respond.

When TikTok emerged as a new platform with kids dancing on it, Bloom took a bet on it while competitors stayed on Facebook and legacy platforms. Bloom built what LaVecchia describes as the largest in-house influencer marketing agency inside a consumer brand, running operations from LA and Austin headquarters. The program accumulated 12 billion+ views across the influencer program.

Greg LaVecchia describes manufacturing proximity to business partners as a deliberate luck-increasing move: when Bloom partnered with Dr. Pepper (based in Texas) and Nutribolt (based in Austin, Texas) to distribute their energy drink, LaVecchia and Mari physically relocated to Austin to be geographically close to those strategic partners. Before that, when building the influencer program, they were in LA where influencer density was highest. In total, they moved five times in five years chasing geographic alignment with business needs.

Bloom launched Shirley Temple energy drink on TikTok Shop before it was available in any retail stores. Without a retail launch, the product sold 14,000 cases (approximately 168,000 cans) directly through TikTok Shop. LaVecchia notes that Red Bull was not on TikTok Shop at the time, and neither were Pepsi, Coke, Dr. Pepper, or Mountain Dew.

practices.text: Every six months, look in the mirror and assess whether you recognize the person looking back; if you do recognize yourself without change, treat it as a signal that you have not leveled up sufficiently.

When trying to get a meeting with a powerful buyer or partner who will be at a specific trade show or city, go to that location even if uninvited; show up in the room where the decision-makers are concentrated.

Share business achievements publicly on social media (retailer milestones, sales records, distribution wins) as a way to attract talent, partners, investors, and retailers who are looking for the next big thing.

When assessing a new opportunity, apply a moonshot filter: only pursue ventures that could realistically be $100M+ opportunities, because the effort required is not proportionally less for smaller opportunities.
Allocate 100% of your mindshare to the most valuable thing you are working on; treat your mind as your most important portfolio and refuse to divide it across multiple ventures simultaneously.

As you transition from one venture to the next, note and archive the specific learnings (consumer preferences, negotiation patterns, supplier relationships, flavor data) from the prior business; these will surface as directly applicable inputs in future challenges at larger scale.
Move out of your hometown and away from any environment where you are the highest-performing person in the room; being a shark in a small pond depresses ambition and reduces luck surface area.
